source_text: Ἐπειδὴ καὶ τὸ ῥεῖν τοῖς ὕδασι διὰ τὸ θεῖον πρόσταγμα, καὶ τὸ εἴσω τῶν ὅρων περιγεγράφθαι τὴν θάλασσαν, ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης ἐστὶ νομοθεσίας· Συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν. Ἵνα μὴ τὸ ἐπιρρέον ὕδωρ τῶν δεχομένων αὐτὸ χωρίων ὑπερχεόμενον, μετεκβαῖνον ἀεὶ καὶ ἄλλα ἐξ ἄλλων πληροῦν, πᾶσαν κατὰ τὸ συνεχὲς ἐπικλύσῃ τὴν ἤπειρον, ἐκελεύσθη συναχθῆναι εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν. Διὰ τοῦτο μαινομένη πολλάκις ἐξ ἀνέμων ἡ θάλασσα, καὶ εἰς ὕψος μέγιστον διανισταμένη τοῖς κύμασιν, ἐπειδὰν μόνον τῶν αἰγιαλῶν ἅψηται, εἰς ἀφρὸν διαλύσασα τὴν ὁρμὴν ἐπανῆλθεν. Ἢ ἐμὲ οὐ φοβηθήσεσθε, λέγει Κύριος, τὸν τιθέντα ἄμμον ὅριον τῇ θαλάσσῃ; Τῷ ἀσθενεστάτῳ πάντων τῇ ψάμμῳ ἡ ταῖς βίαις ἀφόρητος χαλινοῦται. Ἐπεὶ τί ἐκώλυε τὴν ἐρυθρὰν θάλασσαν πᾶσαν τὴν Αἴγυπτον κοιλοτέραν οὖσαν ἑαυτῆς ἐπελθεῖν, καὶ συναφθῆναι τῷ παρακειμένῳ τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ πελάγει, εἰ μὴ τῷ προστάγματι ἦν πεπεδημένη τοῦ κτίσαντος; Ὅτι γὰρ ταπεινοτέρα τῆς ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης ἡ Αἴγυπτος, ἔργῳ ἔπεισαν ἡμᾶς οἱ θελήσαντες ἀλλήλοις τὰ πελάγη συνάψαι, τό τε Αἰγύπτιον καὶ τὸ Ἰνδικὸν, ἐν ᾧ ἡ ἐρυθρά ἐστι θάλασσα. Διόπερ ἐπέσχον τὴν ἐπιχείρησιν, ὅ τε πρῶτος ἀρξάμενος Σέσωστρις ὁ Αἰγύπτιος, καὶ ὁ μετὰ ταῦτα βουληθεὶς ἐπεξεργάσασθαι Δαρεῖος ὁ Μῆδος. Ταῦτα μοι εἴρηται, ἵνα νοήσωμεν τοῦ προστάγματος τὴν δύναμιν· Συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν. Τουτέστιν, ἄλλη ἀπὸ ταύτης μὴ ἀπογενηθήτω, ἀλλ' ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ συλλογῇ ἀπομεινάτω τὸ συναγόμενον. 4.4 Ἔπειτα ὁ εἰπὼν συναχθῆναι τὰ ὕδατα εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν, ἔδειξέ σοι, ὅτι πολλὰ ἦν κατὰ πολλοὺς τόπους διῃρημένα τὰ ὕδατα. Αἵ τε γὰρ τῶν ὀρῶν κοιλότητες, φάραγξι βαθείαις ὑπερρηγμέναι, εἶχον τῶν ὑδάτων τὴν συλλογήν. Καὶ προσέτι πεδία πολλά τε καὶ ὕπτια οὐδὲν τῶν μεγίστων πελαγῶν κατὰ τὸ μέγεθος ἀποδέοντα, καὶ αὐλῶνες μυρίοι, καὶ αἱ κοιλάδες κατ' ἄλλα καὶ ἄλλα σχήματα κοιλαινόμεναι, πάντα ὑδάτων τότε πεπληρωμένα, ἀπεκενώθη τῷ θείῳ προστάγματι, πρὸς μίαν συναγωγὴν τοῦ πανταχόθεν ὕδατος συνελασθέντος. Καὶ μηδεὶς λεγέτω, ὅτι εἴπερ ἦν ὕδωρ ἐπάνω τῆς γῆς, πάντως πᾶσαι αἱ κοιλότητες, αἱ νῦν τὴν θάλασσαν ὑποδεξάμεναι, πεπληρωμέναι ὑπῆρχον. Ποῦ τοίνυν ἔμελλον γίνεσθαι τῶν ὑδάτων αἱ συλλογαὶ, προκατειλημμένων τῶν κοίλων; Πρὸς δὴ τοῦτο ἐροῦμεν, ὅτι τότε καὶ τὰ ἀγγεῖα συγκατεσκευάσθη, ὅτι ἔδει μίαν σύστασιν ἀποκριθῆναι τὸ ὕδωρ. Οὐ γὰρ ἦν ἡ ἔξω Γαδείρων θάλασσα· οὐδὲ τὸ μέγα ἐκεῖνο καὶ ἀτόλμητον πλωτῆρσι πέλαγος, τὸ τὴν Βρεττανικὴν νῆσον καὶ τοὺς ἑσπερίους Ἴβηρας περιπτυσσόμενον· ἀλλὰ τότε τῆς εὐρυχωρίας τῷ προστάγματι τοῦ Θεοῦ δημιουργηθείσης, ἐπ' αὐτὴν συνεδόθη τῶν ὑδάτων τὰ πλήθη. Πρὸς δὲ τὸ, ὅτι ὑπεναντίως ἔχει τῇ πείρᾳ ὁ τῆς παρ' ἡμῖν κοσμοποιίας λόγος (οὐ γὰρ εἰς μίαν συναγωγὴν ὑδάτων τὸ ὕδωρ ἅπαν φαίνεται συνδραμόν), πολλὰ μέν ἐστιν εἰπεῖν, καὶ πᾶσιν αὐτόθεν γνώριμα. Μήποτε δὲ καὶ τὸ διαμάχεσθαι τοῖς τοιούτοις γελοῖον. Οὐ δήπου γὰρ καὶ τὰ τελματιαῖα, καὶ τὰ ἐξ ὄμβρων συναθροιζόμενα προφέρειν ἡμῖν ὀφείλουσι, καὶ διὰ τούτων τὸν λόγον ἡμῶν ἐλέγχειν οἴεσθαι; Ἀλλὰ τὴν μεγίστην καὶ τελεωτάτην συνδρομὴν τῶν ὑδάτων ὠνόμασε συναγωγὴν μίαν.
thought_title: The sea's boundary is God's command
orientation: Basil is expounding the command 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering' from Genesis 1:9, arguing that the sea's limits are fixed by divine decree, not by nature.
pass_a_gloss: Since both the flowing of the waters is due to the divine command, and the sea being bounded within limits is from the first legislation: 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.' So that the water flowing in, overflowing the places that receive it, always passing over and filling one place after another, might not flood the whole continent continuously, it was commanded to be gathered into one gathering. Because of this the sea, often raging from winds and rising up to a very great height with its waves, whenever it only touches the shores, having dissolved its force into foam, returns. 'Or will you not fear me, says the Lord, who sets sand as a boundary to the sea?' By the weakest of all things, by sand, the one unbearable in its forces is bridled. Since what prevented the Red Sea from coming over all Egypt, which is lower than itself, and being joined to the sea lying beside Egypt, if it had not been bound by the command of the Creator? For that Egypt is lower than the Red Sea, those who wished to join the seas to one another persuaded us by deed, both the Egyptian sea and the Indian sea, in which the Red Sea is. Therefore they stopped the attempt, both the first who began it, Sesostris the Egyptian, and the one who later wished to complete it, Darius the Mede. These things have been said by me, so that we may understand the power of the command: 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.' That is, let no other gathering be produced from this one, but let what is gathered remain in the first collection. Then the one who said that the waters be gathered into one gathering showed you that the waters were many, divided in many places. For the hollows of the mountains, broken open with deep ravines, held the collection of the waters. And in addition many flat and level plains, lacking nothing of the greatest seas in size, and countless valleys, and the hollows being hollowed out in different and different shapes, all then filled with waters, were emptied by the divine command, the water from everywhere being driven together to one gathering. And let no one say that if there was water above the earth, certainly all the hollows, the ones now receiving the sea, were filled. Where then were the gatherings of the waters going to be, the hollows being already occupied? To this indeed we will say, that then also the vessels were prepared together, because the water had to be separated off as one mass. For the sea outside Gades was not; nor that great sea, untried by sailors, which embraces the British island and the western Iberians; but then, when the broad space was created by the command of God, the masses of the waters were gathered together into it. But as to the fact that the account of the world-making among us is contrary to experience (for not all the water appears to have run together into one gathering of waters), there is much to say, and all things known to everyone from this very fact. But perhaps even to fight against such people is ridiculous. For surely they ought not to bring forward the marshy waters and the waters gathered from rains, and think to refute our account through these? But he named the greatest and most complete running together of the waters 'one gathering.'

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of the Genesis command as Basil quotes it, preserving the noun 'gathering' rather than a more idiomatic 'place' or 'reservoir'
Passive aorist emphasizes the divine command as the agent of the waters' gathering, matching Basil's argument that this is legislation from God
The metaphor of a bridle on a horse conveys the sea's violent force being restrained by the weakest thing, sand; 'bridled' preserves the image
The perfect passive participle of πεδάω (to fetter) conveys a continuing state of being held fast by the Creator's command
The adjective ἀτόλμητος means 'not dared,' and with the dative πλωτῆρσι it means sailors had not dared to attempt it; 'untried by sailors' captures this
The noun συνδρομή literally means a running together or confluence; keeping the verbal force shows Basil distinguishing the great gathering from small pools

pass_b_english: The flowing of the waters and the sea's confinement within its boundaries both come from that first legislation: "Let the waters be gathered into one gathering" (Genesis 1:9). The water that kept flowing in would have overflowed the places that received it, always moving on and filling one place after another, until it flooded the whole continent in an unbroken sweep. So it was commanded to be gathered into one gathering. That is why the sea, even when it rages under the winds and its waves rear up to an enormous height, the moment it touches the shore, dissolves its force into foam and turns back. "Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea?" (Jeremiah 5:22). The sea, whose violence cannot be withstood, is bridled by the weakest thing of all—sand. What else kept the Red Sea from sweeping over all Egypt, which lies lower than the sea itself, and joining the ocean that borders Egypt, if it was not bound by the command of its Creator? That Egypt is lower than the Red Sea has been proved to us in practice by those who wanted to join the two seas to each other—the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, in which the Red Sea lies. That is why they abandoned the attempt: first Sesostris the Egyptian, who began it, and then Darius the Mede, who later wanted to carry it through. I have said all this so that we may understand the power of the command: "Let the waters be gathered into one gathering." That is, let no other gathering be produced from this one, but let what is gathered remain in that first collection.

Then the one who said that the waters should be gathered into one gathering showed you that the waters had been many, divided among many places. The hollows of the mountains, split by deep ravines, held their own collections of water. And in addition, many broad and level plains, no smaller in extent than the greatest seas, and countless valleys and basins hollowed out in every kind of shape—all of them, filled with water at that time, were emptied by the divine command, as the water from every direction was driven together into one gathering. And let no one say: if there was water above the earth, then surely all the hollows that now hold the sea must already have been full. Where, then, were the gatherings of the waters going to form, if the hollows were already occupied? To this we will answer that the vessels were prepared at that very time, when the water had to be set apart into one mass. For the sea beyond Cadiz did not yet exist, nor that great ocean untried by sailors, which embraces the island of Britain and the western Iberians. But at that time, when the wide expanse was created by God's command, the masses of water were gathered together into it.

As for the objection that our account of the world's making contradicts experience—since not all the water appears to have run together into one gathering—there is much to say, and it is obvious to everyone. Perhaps it is even ridiculous to argue against such objections. Surely they do not mean to bring up marsh water and rainwater collected in pools, and think they are refuting our argument with these? No, he called the greatest and most complete running together of the waters "one gathering."

last_rejected.quote: "Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea?"
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἢ ἐμὲ οὐ φοβηθήσεσθε, λέγει Κύριος, τὸν τιθέντα ἄμμον ὅριον τῇ θαλάσσῃ;
last_rejected.why: English hides that God speaks; "says the Lord" buried mid-quote makes it seem like Basil's words.
last_rejected.fix: "Will you not fear me?" says the Lord. "I am the one who set the sand as a boundary for the sea."
last_rejected.ruling: 'says the Lord' (λέγει Κύριος) is present in the English; placement is a stylistic choice, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: Source says Darius was a Mede, but this is Darius I of Persia (Hystaspes), not 'the Mede' of Daniel.
last_rejected.ruling: Source says 'Δαρεῖος ὁ Μῆδος' = 'Darius the Mede'; translation faithfully renders it. Historical identity is not the translator's concern.

last_rejected.quote: the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, in which the Red Sea lies
last_rejected.source_quote: τό τε Αἰγύπτιον καὶ τὸ Ἰνδικὸν, ἐν ᾧ ἡ ἐρυθρά ἐστι θάλασσα
last_rejected.why: Greek says Red Sea lies in the Indian Ocean, not that Indian Ocean contains Red Sea; 'in which' refers back to Indian Ocean.
last_rejected.fix: the Egyptian Sea and the Indian Ocean, in which the Red Sea lies
last_rejected.ruling: 'ἐν ᾧ ἡ ἐρυθρά ἐστι θάλασσα' = 'in which the Red Sea lies'; English correctly says Red Sea lies in the Indian Ocean.

last_rejected.source_quote: ὑπερχεόμενον, μετεκβαῖνον ἀεὶ καὶ ἄλλα ἐξ ἄλλων πληροῦν, πᾶσαν κατὰ τὸ συνεχὲς ἐπικλύσῃ τὴν ἤπειρον
last_rejected.why: Greek states purpose/result (ἵνα μὴ...ἐπικλύσῃ), not a counterfactual; 'would have' weakens the divine prevention.
last_rejected.fix: so that the flowing water, overflowing the places that received it, always moving on and filling one place after another, might not flood the whole continent in an unbroken sweep
last_rejected.ruling: Greek ἵνα μὴ...ἐπικλύσῃ is purpose clause; 'would have overflowed' conveys the prevented result adequately. No meaning lost.
